::: {#sol-smooth-loss}

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
c_log = cutoffs[log_loss.argmin()]
error_at_c_log = np.mean((ink_01 > c_log) != is_one)
print(c_log, log_loss.min(), error_at_c_log)
```

Yes.
The curve in @fig-log-loss-curve is smooth, with one lowest point,
and its slope points downhill from every other cutoff,
so gradient descent has a direction to follow.

The lowest [log loss](https://morrison-lab.github.io/lds/chapters/logistic-regression.html#def-log-loss) is at $c$ = `r sprintf("%.2f", py$c_log)`.
The hard rule with that cutoff gets `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * py$error_at_c_log)`% of the 0s and 1s wrong,
against the lowest possible `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * min(py$error_rate))`% from @sol-train-on-errors.
Minimizing the log loss does not minimize the [error rate](https://morrison-lab.github.io/lds/chapters/metrics.html#def-error-rate) exactly,
but it comes close, and it can be done by gradient descent.

Deep networks are trained the same way:
on a smooth loss such as the log loss, which is also called cross-entropy,
while their error rate or accuracy is what gets reported.

:::
